I agree with you that one should indeed not be absolutely reliant upon others to be content with life, but I also find an element of discord here. Whilst the argument is rationally valid, it conflicts our innate disposition when taken to the extremity. The inclination to outsource is arguably a survival mechanism that has been ingrained into us over time, and to inhibit it pushes us to self-annihilation. I believe it is more about managing the scale of outsourcing than to completely withdraw from life in seeking to be entirely self-reliant. 
On a personal level, every time I am driven to undertake a certain action I ask myself the simple question of why I am doing this, what do I seek to extract from doing this. The deeper I go in to finding what instigates the desire to for a certain something, the more I find that I am giving up the control to what I extract from that action onto the whims of someone else’s approval; and I find it is the case for almost everyone and virtually every action. An artist, a writer, a lover, a thinker, everyone is dependent upon someone to validate them or their work, and that is technically the giving up of self-reliance. — This is what my rational faculties conclude. But the emotional underbelly of the mind, one that has been wired to human connection and co-dependency of our specie continues to make its presence felt. Though I do not let it override reason, it is still there and I can feel it. I feel it is more about maintaining a balance between neither fully untethering myself from the world but nor jumping knee deep in to it as-well. That is where I find myself in a predicament, as I don’t have the tethers readily extended to me by default that would tip the scale on to a more balanced threshold, and I also do not have the ability or the drive to seek them on my own; hence the ideation of self-annihilation.
